doc.title: Ruth Lion interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

title: Japan tribute and Blue Note Festival
summary: The Japanese tribute reunited Alfred with many Blue Note friends; he insisted on going despite illness, including to the Mount Fuji festival.

blocks.x: That was a magnificent time of his life. I know that meant the world to him. Here he is. And these are the guys, so many of the guys that he loved. There’s Bruce Lundwall. I don’t think Michael Cuscuna — Bobby Hutcherson, Kenny Burrell, Jimmy Smith, so many of the guys. And so he went through that. It was an ordeal. But the last day that we were there, Reid Miles by the way went over on the plane with us, which was wonderful because Reid was a riot. This guy, he was absolutely as wild as Alfred and Frank. And these are like wild men I’m talking about. They were just not the average person. But anyway, that last day, Leonard Feather who was our close, dear friend, and a number of people were giving us a go-away breakfast. And among those people were five people from Japan, who we knew had attended the concert. But we didn’t know particularly who © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

they were. And so they were very kind to us and everything. And then we went back home and he got word that they would like to have the Blue Note Festival at Mount Fuji. Well right away I said, “Alfred, no way, we can’t do that.” I mean we want to live, don’t we? Well I’ll have to show you this picture of him when his 70 — this was after cardiac arrest, I want to show you how good he looked, with the little blue suit on. He was a dandy, you know? This guy loved clothes. And so you see you remember that song Elvis used to sing, the “Blue Suede Shoes?” There they are too.

And he had been — but anyway we celebrated his birthday and we went over to our favorite place in LaJolla and celebrated. And I have a hundred pictures of Alfred. But anyway, these guys told him that they wanted him to come and they were going to have the Blue Note Festival at Mount Fuji. And I just had to be as firm as I could, “We’re not going to do it.” Well he went, you know he knew I liked him to dress up, which he loved to dress up anyway. He went and he got himself all gorgeous. And we had a little patio. And I’m sitting there, and he comes out on the patio and he puts his hands on his hips, and he says, “I don’t know about you, maybe you’re not going, but I’m going to Japan.” Well I couldn’t say no.

He looked too fabulous with his little outfit that he had on, he had beige, and that was my favorite color on him, and he loved blue. And so I just said well I can’t win this one, and I have to let it go, and so we went. And it was very difficult because he got ill on the plane and we had to sit down in Hawaii and stay there for three days while he got better, and then we went to there and they were kind enough to have a medical doctor in the suite next to us, who was on call 24 hours, stayed with us and saw that he had oxygen and everything. But he went through that whole — this picture here, this one I’d like to show, this was in a restaurant they took us to. Now this guy, this doesn’t look like a mortally ill person, does it. He died three months later. But at that festival, Herbie Hancock was there, Lou Donaldson was there, they got everybody that Alfred loved. And it was wonderful. But three thousand people got up and gave him a standing ovation. And I think that’s why I have heard it said that that’s why he didn’t die August 8th from that cardiac arrest. That he would have that. Because there are no fans, in my opinion, like the Japanese fans. They knew the song — I mean whatever it was they’d be going along with the song and everything. It was wonderful. And the people who were there, Dr. Ogawa and Mr. Namacoti and gee I can’t recall at the moment, it was like a life beyond life. And so those people will always live in my heart, if I can’t remember their names. © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

Well gee, that’s, and you’ve had, since Alfred passed, you have gotten into another dimension of entertainment with your Cable Access work, and I wanted to congratulate you on your award, from the PACE organization.
